prose.summary: An architect turns a client's program and budget into construction documents that a contractor can actually build, then stays on through construction administration to make sure the built thing matches the drawings. That last part is what separates the role from an architectural drafter, who produces the documents but rarely owns the client relationship or the code compliance. Revit and construction administration together account for a third of what these postings ask for, which tells you the job is drawing plus oversight, not drawing alone.
prose.judgement: The pay band is wide: a quarter of postings land at $76k or below, a quarter at $121k or above, and the difference tracks firm size and licensure more than raw skill. A 3.3 percent yearly switch rate is low for a design field, meaning people who get in tend to stay, for better or worse. Education is a hard filter here (60 percent of postings require it outright), and remote work barely exists at 12 percent, so this is still a drafting-table-adjacent, in-office trade whatever the software stack suggests. The honest part: if you want out, the fast lateral moves (Interior Designer, Architectural Drafter) pay less than what you're leaving, and the ones that pay comparably (Structural Engineer, Civil Engineer) want another license and another year or two first.
prose.who_qualifies: Interior Designers and Architectural Drafters carry the highest measured match into this role, both around 54 percent, because they already speak in construction documents, code references, and client presentations. MEP Engineers (45 percent) and BIM Manager (41 percent) bring the model-coordination half of the job, Revit and BIM specifically, without the design-authorship half. Structural and Civil Engineers show up lower, at 33 and 32 percent, which fits: they know the building codes and the construction administration but not the presentation or design development work architects are also measured on.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: A posting can tell you a firm wants Revit and five years of experience; it cannot tell you whether the studio culture rewards design ambition or just punches out permit sets. None of the tracked skills capture the licensing exam sequence itself, which is the actual bottleneck for anyone trying to move into the licensed roles this data shows as exits. And a listed salary band says nothing about whether a small firm's $76k is negotiable or a hard ceiling.

faq.q: Do I need a professional degree to get hired as an architect?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases: 60 percent of postings state it as a requirement outright, with another 14 percent listing it as preferred. Only 10 percent waive it, so this is one of the firmer gates in the field rather than something experience alone substitutes for.

faq.q: Which software should I prioritize if I'm trying to get noticed?
faq.a: Revit shows up in 34 percent of postings, well ahead of anything else, so it's the baseline expectation rather than a differentiator. Rhino, Bluebeam, and ArchiCAD each sit around 14 percent and function more as tie-breakers once Revit is assumed.

faq.q: Can I do this job remotely?
faq.a: Not typically. Only 12 percent of live postings offer remote work, which tracks with a role that includes construction administration and site visits as core duties, not occasional ones.

faq.q: If I want to leave architecture, what's the fastest realistic move?
faq.a: Interior Designer is the quickest and highest-match exit, at 64 percent match and 9 to 16 months, with no license required, though the pay band ($55k to $90k) sits below typical architect salaries. Moves into licensed adjacent fields like Civil or Structural Engineer pay closer to what you're likely earning now, but they run 12 to 24 months plus a separate license.
